title: The work integral has an observable endpoint
question: What energy is required to accelerate an electron?
recap: Adding up the work of the force along the motion, from rest to speed v, gives the electron’s kinetic energy, mc²(γ − 1). Einstein then gives two more relations a laboratory can test: the voltage that accelerates the electron, and how sharply electric and magnetic fields bend its path.
premises: The electron has a fixed mass m and moves slower than light, and force is defined as stated.
For the voltage relation, the electron starts at rest and all the work of the field becomes its energy of motion.
limitations: Losses by radiation and interactions with matter are left out.
The kinetic energy formula alone does not give the September paper’s result that a body’s mass changes with its energy.

overview.text: Adding up the work of the force along the motion, from rest to speed \(v\), gives the electron’s kinetic energy, \(mc^2(\gamma - 1)\). Einstein then gives two more relations a laboratory can test: the voltage that accelerates the electron, and how sharply electric and magnetic fields bend its path.

full.spoken: Integrating the longitudinal work from rest gives m c squared times gamma minus one.

full.text: The integral follows from one derivative, \(d\gamma/du = \gamma^3 u/c^2\): the integrand \(m\gamma^3 u\) is \(mc^2\) times it, so the integral is \(mc^2(\gamma - 1)\). At low speed this approaches the familiar \(mv^2/2\). At \(0.6c\) the exact value is \(0.25\,mc^2\) and the low-speed formula gives \(0.18\,mc^2\), a difference large enough to see.

full.spoken: For acceleration from rest, charge magnitude times voltage magnitude supplies kinetic energy; in a transverse magnetic field the circular radius is gamma m v over charge magnitude B.

full.text: The third relation compares bending by the two kinds of field. In an electric field across the motion the path curves with radius \(\gamma mv^2/(|q|E)\) at that instant; the field also speeds the electron up as the path turns, so the radius keeps changing. In a magnetic field the speed stays constant and the path is a circle of radius \(\gamma mv/(|q|B)\). The electron-dynamics laboratory keeps the two cases apart.

full.returnCaption: Return to the energy it takes to accelerate an electron.

steps.text: Letters: the paper's electron has charge ε and mass μ (m here); it starts at rest at the origin of K and moves along the X axis under an electrostatic force X; W is its energy of motion, P the potential difference it has passed through, its magnetic and electric deflectabilities \(A_m\) and \(A_e\), R the radius of curvature of its path, N a magnetic force across its motion, and V the speed of light.

items: The energy taken from the electrostatic field is \(\intε X\,dx\). The electron is accelerated slowly and so gives off no energy as radiation, so that energy all becomes its energy of motion W.
The first of equations (A) holds throughout: \(ε X=\mu\beta^3\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}\). Along the path, acceleration times a small distance is \(v\,dv\), so \(ε X\,dx=\mu\beta^3v\,dv\).

Integrate from rest to speed v, using \(\frac{d}{dv}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/V^2}}=\frac{v}{V^2}\beta^3\): the paper's result \(W=\mu V^2\left\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}}-1\right\}\). In the explanatory letters, the formula below.

steps.spoken: Integrating the longitudinal work from rest gives m c squared times gamma minus one.

items: At low speed, \(1/\sqrt{1-ε}\) is about \(1+ε/2\), so W approaches \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\).

Worked at 0.6c: exact \((1.25-1)mc^2=0.25\,mc^2\); low-speed \(0.5\times0.36\,mc^2=0.18\,mc^2\). For an electron, with modern SI constants, \(mc^2\) is about 511 kiloelectronvolts, so W is about 127.7 kiloelectronvolts.
W becomes infinite at v = V. The paper concludes, as from its earlier results, that speeds greater than light have no possibility of existence.

The paper lists three properties of the motion that experiment can reach. First: an electric force Y and a magnetic force N deflect an electron moving at v equally when \(Y=N\,v/V\), so the ratio of magnetic to electric deflectability gives the speed, \(A_m/A_e=v/V\), and the speed can be measured independently.

Second: the potential difference passed through and the speed gained are related by \(P=\int X\,dx=\frac{\mu}{ε}V^2\left\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}}-1\right\}\). In SI, charge times voltage equals W. Worked: to reach 0.6c from rest, an electron needs about 128 kilovolts, with no energy lost to radiation.

Third: the radius of curvature R when a magnetic force N across the motion is the only deflecting force. From the second of (A), \(v^2/R=\frac{ε}{\mu}\frac{v}{V}N\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\), so \(R=V^2\frac{\mu}{ε}\frac{v/V}{\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}}\frac{1}{N}\). In SI that is \(r_B=\gamma mv/(|q|B)\), the second formula below.

steps.spoken: For acceleration from rest, charge magnitude times voltage magnitude supplies kinetic energy; in a transverse magnetic field the circular radius is gamma m v over charge magnitude B.

items: Worked: an electron at 0.6c in a field of 0.1 tesla circles with radius \(1.25\times m\times0.6c/(|q|\times0.1)\), about 1.28 centimetres, with modern SI constants.
Keep the magnetic case, a circle at constant speed, apart from bending in an electric field, which also changes the speed and so gives a radius that holds only at one instant.

The paper calls these three relations a complete expression of the laws by which, according to the theory, the electron must move. They hold within its assumptions: the fields as specified, and no energy lost to radiation.
The kinetic energy formula alone does not give the September paper's result that a body's mass changes with its energy content; that needs the argument from the light complex of §8.

steps.returnCaption: Return to the energy it takes to accelerate an electron.

margin.text: The three relations hold within the model’s assumptions: fields as specified, and no energy lost to radiation. After §10 the paper closes with thanks to M. Besso and the date line, Bern, June 1905. Those belong to the German source text, and this explanation does not repeat them.
